previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder, alcoholic cirrhosis, and opioid use disorder was admitted for alcohol withdrawal after relapsing and consuming large amounts of vodka daily for six days. He presented with tremors, abdominal pain, vomiting with blood streaks, visual disturbances, and altered mental status. He was managed with a phenobarbital taper in the ICU, transitioned to the general floor, and completed detoxification. Hepatic encephalopathy was treated with lactulose and rifaximin, with improvement in mental status. Hepatopulmonary syndrome was diagnosed via echocardiogram and confirmed on CT angiogram, but oxygen levels improved with activity, avoiding home oxygen. Pancytopenia and portal hypertension were noted on imaging and labs, with no acute bleeding. He was restarted on buprenorphine, received hepatitis vaccinations, and was discharged home with plans for a dual diagnosis day program, follow-up with hepatology, and strict alcohol abstinence.

Brief Hospital Course:
SUMMARY
=============== 
___ year old male with EtOH cirrhosis and severe asthma presented 
with abdominal pain, upper back pain, anxiousness, and chest 
tightness found to have acute hypoxemic respiratory failure from 
asthma exacerbation with short admission to the MICU for 
monitoring with continuous albuterol nebs, duonebs, IV 
magnesium, IV antibiotics, and IV methylprednisolone, 
transferred to medicine for further management. Sputum culture 
grew H influenza and patient was narrowed to ceftriaxone from 
broad-spectrum antibiotics. On the medicine service steroids 
were tapered and he was diuresed aggressively with IV furosemide 
for fluid overload which likely occurred in the setting of 
high-dose steroids. In addition psychiatry recommended an opioid 
pain regimen that he could take while on Suboxone. Pulmonology 
team was consulted for management of his asthma exacerbation and 
recommended a prednisone taper as well as starting Spiriva and 
various nebulizers. He was weaned off his additional pain 
medications back to his Suboxone which he was discharged on 
twice daily. Sertraline was initiated for anxiety.

ACUTE ISSUES
===============
# Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure
# Asthma Exacerbation
# Community-acquired pneumonia
# Acute pulmonary edema
Patient presented with hypoxia, wheezing c/w severe asthma 
exacerbation. Admitted to MICU and treated with IV steroids, IV 
magnesium, nebs. Did not require intubation, but continued to 
have ongoing dyspnea and marked diffuse wheezing on exam. 
Transferred to floor for further management. Chest CT 
subsequently revealed new bilateral GGOs c/f HAP contributory to 
ongoing hypoxia. He was initiated on vancomycin and ceftaz, 
these were narrowed to ceftriaxone after cultures came back as 
ampicillin sensitive h flu. With respect to asthma management, 
transitioned from IV methylprednisolone to PO prednisone 100MG. 
This was decreased to 60 and then decreased on a prednisone 
taper every 4 days. He also developed extreme fluid overload in 
the setting of steroid therapy. He was aggressively diuresed 
with IV Lasix, and his spironolactone dose was increased to 150 
twice daily. Once he resumed euvolemic he was switched back to 
his home Lasix 80 mg twice daily and spironolactone 100 mg twice 
daily. However, he developed mild ___ so diuretics where 
switched to daily dosing. His weights will need to be monitored 
to see if initiation of BID dosing. 

#Hyponatremia
#Hyperkalemia
Patient developed hyponatremia and hyperkalemia while on the 
medicine service. Hyponatremia was thought due to fluid overload 
in the setting of cirrhosis, high dose of steroids. Hyperkalemia 
occurred in the setting of baseline normal renal function, 
thought possibly due to increased dose of spironolactone. There 
was concern for adrenal insufficiency in the setting of steroid 
taper, however we believe that these doses of steroids are too 
high for adrenal insufficiency to cause these electrolyte 
derangements. Hyponatremia and hyperkalemia improved with 
diuresis, spironolactone dose was decreased to home dose, home 
Lasix was resumed once patient euvolemic. Due to mild AK I and 
ongoing hyponatremia prior to discharge, Lasix and 
spironolactone dosing were changed to once daily from twice 
daily.

# EtOH cirrhosis:
Child B. Complicated by HE, hepatopulmonary syndrome, 
thrombocytopenia (plts 54, baseline). MELD-Na 14 on transfer out 
of MICU. RUQUS negative for ascites. On lasix, spironolactone as 
outpatient as well as a stress potassium supplementation; may 
reflect underdosing of spironolactone or overdosing of lasix, as 
current dose ratio >2:5 of lasix: spironolactone (which would 
expect to result in hypokalemia requiring supplementation). 
Increased spironolactone to 150 on ___. Given hypervolemia on 
exam, orthopnea noted on
___, switched to IV Lasix for active diuresis. MELD-Na stable 
at 14.

# Chronic pain
Patient reported increased pain in back, shoulder, chest. 
Symptoms appear consistent with prior chronic pain symptoms, 
which have been treated symptomatically as outpatient with 
gabapentin, methocarbamol, suboxone. Also started tylenol (<2g 
daily), lidocaine patch. Per addiction psych, for pain control 
decreased suboxone to once daily and started PO dilaudid ___ 
q8H PRN for dyspnea, breakthrough pain. Was weaned off dilaudid 
and started back on BID suboxone in conjunction with his PCP 
___. He was discharged on BID lorazopam 0.25 mg 
BID:PRN for anxiety. We called his PCP and they confirmed ok to 
prescribe lorazopam going forward. 

# HFpEF
TTE ___ with EF 64%. Noted to have worsening volume overload 
on exam in days following MICU transfer, likely fluid retention 
in setting of IV steroids contributing to orthopnea as above. 
Actively diuresed with IV Lasix with good UOP.

# Chest Tightness
Likely secondary to bronchospasm given evidence of severe asthma 
exacerbation, continued diffuse wheezes on exam. Low suspicion 
for cardiac ischemia given overall risk profile, absence of 
suggestive EKG findings. EKG not suggestive of pericarditis.

# Epigastric pain
Likely secondary to labored breathing. RUQUS negative for 
ascites, low suspicion for SBP. No GI symptoms. ___ also be 
component of GERD. Asthma exacerbation managed as above, 
continued on PPI for GERD and ulcer prophylaxis while on 
high-dose steroids.

# Thrush
On day of discharge patient noted mouth pain, exam was 
consistent with oral candidiasis. Patient was given clotrimazole 
troches.

CHRONIC ISSUES 
=============== 
# Anxiety
# Insomnia
Patient reports continued anxiety. Received IV Ativan in ED with 
some response. As this has been a chronic issue for patient, 
prefer to limit benzodiazepines, continue current outpatient 
regimen with hydroxyzine PRN for acute anxiety. Patient denied 
recent alcohol use. IV steroids likely contributory to acute 
worsening of anxiety/insomnia, although at this time given 
severe asthma exacerbation benefits of steroids outweigh risks. 
Continued home clonidine, seroquel, trazodone, also started 
hydroxyzine and ativan for symptom control. Started sertraline 
at 25 mg daily. He was discharged on BID lorazopam 0.25 mg 
BID:PRN for anxiety after discussion with his PCP.

# Alcohol use disorder:
Complicated by withdrawal and DTs in the past. Two 
hospitalizations last year for withdrawal. Patient reports last 
drink of alcohol 6 months, 3 weeks ago. Continued FoLIC Acid 1 
mg PO DAILY, Multivitamins 1 TAB PO DAILY, Thiamine 100 mg PO 
DAILY. 

# Opiate use disorder:
Patient reported that he had been self tapering and only taking 
suboxone once daily. Continued suboxone, with dose reduction to 
daily to allow for acute pain management as above. Per 
discussion with primary care physician, patient should have 
continued to take Suboxone twice daily so was discharged on this 
regimen.

INDICATION:  ___ year old male with EtOH cirrhosis and severe asthma presented
with hypoxemic respiratory failure concerning for asthma exacerbation with s/p

PLEURA: There is no pleural effusion.
LUNG:

1. PARENCHYMA:  Newly developed parenchymal areas of ground-glass opacities
involving all pulmonary lobes, more prominent in the central and perihilar

Newly developed ground-glass opacities involving both lungs.  Main diagnostic
considerations include infective changes (viral or atypical infection),
interstitial disease (COP or AIP), as well as medicamentous etiology and
hypersensitivity pneumonitis.  It is felt to be less likely due to
